kunyah: Abu ad-Darda — his name was Uwaymir
tribe: Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj — Ansar of Madina
teaser: He was among the last of his people to accept Islam, and he ended up teaching the Qur'an to a city.

layers.title: Who
layers.subtitle: A trader from a family that was already at Badr
layers.content:
His name was 'Uwaymir, of the Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj. Reports differ over his father's name. Everyone knows him by his kunya, taken from his daughter ad-Darda'.

He was a merchant in Madina, and by the accounts of him a working one, not a man of leisure.

There is something worth noticing in where he does and does not appear. Ibn Sa'd's volume on the men of Badr names his maternal uncles in full: Subay' ibn Qays and 'Ubada ibn Qays, said to have been twins, of the people of the mosque at Sunh, both present at Badr and at Uhud. Abu ad-Darda' himself is not in the roll. He surfaces in that whole volume twice — once as their nephew, and once as a man standing in a gathering who hears somebody ask, 'Is there not among you the keeper of the secrets?'

So begin with this. His family was already inside the story. He was outside it, in a shop, in the same small town, while the men he was related to went out to Badr and came back.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — entries 213 and 214, Subay' ibn Qays and 'Ubada ibn Qays, described there as the uncles of Abu ad-Darda'; his own notice falls in Ibn Sa'd's later volume on the Companions who settled in Syria

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: He shut the business rather than run both
layers.content:
Reports place him among the last of his people to enter Islam. He was not at Badr. Uhud is given as his first battle.

That is an uncomfortable fact and it is his, so it should be said plainly rather than hurried past. He watched the first years from the edge. Men of his own household had already staked everything before he moved.

When he did move, he moved completely. The saying transmitted from him about that period is one of the most quoted things he ever said: he became Muslim while he was a trader, he tried to hold trade and worship together, the two would not sit in the same pair of hands, so he abandoned trade.

Read it carefully, because it is not a sermon against commerce. He does not say trade is unlawful and he does not tell anyone else to close their stall. He says these two would not combine in him. It is a statement about his own capacity, made by a man who had tested it and found the answer he did not want.

He was late. Then he was more thorough than almost anybody.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra — the notice on Abu ad-Darda' among the Companions of Syria; the report on abandoning trade for worship is among the best known transmitted from him. Note: Vol. III, which covers the men of Badr, does not include him, consistent with the reports that he accepted Islam after Badr

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: Paired with a Persian, and pulled back from himself
layers.content:
The Prophet ﷺ joined him in brotherhood with Salman al-Farisi. Look at the pairing. An Ansari trader of al-Khazraj and a Persian who had been passed from owner to owner before he was freed. Nothing in common except the thing they were both there for.

The reports about that brotherhood all turn on the same episode: Salman came to visit and found Abu ad-Darda' fasting through the days and standing through the nights and letting his household go untended, and it was Salman who pulled him back. The friendship was not made of agreement. It was made of one man being willing to tell the other that he had gone too far.

The principle behind that correction is stated by the Prophet ﷺ in a narration whose companion was someone else — he said to 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As: fast and break your fast, pray and sleep, your body has a right over you.

And this is what Abu ad-Darda' himself carried out of those years, in his own narration: the supplication of a Muslim for his absent brother is answered, and at his head is an angel appointed who says each time, and for you the same.

The man remembered for a brotherhood is the man through whom that hadith reaches us.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim, Book of Remembrance and Supplication, narrated by Abu ad-Darda' — the supplication for an absent brother; the words on fasting and sleeping are in Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Fasting, narrated by 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, and are not narrated of Abu ad-Darda'
layers.source: Sahih Muslim, Book of Remembrance and Supplication; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Fasting; the brotherhood with Salman al-Farisi and the visit are reported in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, in his notice among the Companions of Syria

layers.title: The Trial and Quality
layers.subtitle: Sent to the richest province he had walked away from
layers.content:
Consider what happened to him next, and how badly matched it looks.

Here is a man who had shut his own business because he could not carry trade and worship at once. Syria was then opened, and Damascus became one of the wealthiest cities in the new empire, filling with garrison soldiers, tribute, plunder and converts by the thousand. Abu ad-Darda' was sent there and made a judge — reports differ over which caliph appointed him — and set to teaching the Qur'an in its mosque.

So the man who could not hold two things in his hands was handed a docket of other people's money and a city's worth of students. He did not get the desert. He got the market, permanently, from the bench.

He did it with his wife. Umm ad-Darda' taught in Damascus alongside him and went on teaching after he was gone, and men of the generation after the Companions sat in front of her.

His renunciation, in the end, was not a withdrawal from work. He gave up owning things and spent the rest of his life adjudicating who owned what.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra — the notice on Abu ad-Darda' among the Companions who settled in Syria, including his judgeship at Damascus, on which the reports differ as to the appointing caliph; the teaching of Umm ad-Darda' at Damascus is reported in the biographical literature on the Successors

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: 'The scholars are the inheritors of the prophets'
layers.content:
He died at Damascus. Reports differ on the year, and 32 AH is the one most often given.

What came out of him is a hadith. He is the Companion who transmitted it, and if you have ever heard it read out at the start of a class or printed inside the cover of a book, you have heard him: whoever travels a path seeking knowledge, Allah places him on a path to the Garden. The angels lower their wings for the student of knowledge. The scholars are the inheritors of the prophets, and the prophets left no gold or silver — they left knowledge, so whoever takes it has taken an ample share.

Sit with the shape of that for a moment. The man who could not make trade and worship agree in the same pair of hands, who closed his shop and went to sit in a mosque, is the narrator through whom the ummah received the hadith that says the inheritance of the prophets is not money.

He did not arrive early and he did not die in battle and there is not much preserved about his face or his voice. He is one of the Companions whose legacy is almost entirely other people: a wife who kept teaching, a city that kept reciting, and a line of transmission that has not stopped since. May Allah be pleased with him.
layers.hadith_ref: Sunan Abu Dawud, Book of Knowledge, narrated by Abu ad-Darda' — 'the scholars are the inheritors of the prophets'; also in Sunan at-Tirmidhi and Sunan Ibn Majah
layers.source: Sunan Abu Dawud, Book of Knowledge; the year of death from Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, notice on Abu ad-Darda' among the Companions of Syria, where the reports differ

quiz.prompt: How does Abu ad-Darda appear in Ibn Sa'd's volume on the men of Badr?

options.text: As one of the commanders of the right flank
Only as the nephew of two Badr participants, and once as a listener in a gathering
As the youngest man present
He is given a full entry among the Ansar

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III — entries 213 and 214
quiz.scholar_reflection: His uncles Subay' and 'Ubada ibn Qays are named in full, with their lineage, their children and their battles. He is a clause in their entry.

quiz.prompt: What did Abu ad-Darda say about combining trade and worship?

options.text: That trade was unlawful for a believer
That he expanded his business to fund the poor
That the two would not come together in him, so he abandoned trade
That he traded only in Ramadan

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra — notice on Abu ad-Darda' among the Companions of Syria
quiz.scholar_reflection: The wording is about himself, not about commerce. He tested his own capacity and reported the result, without legislating it for anyone else.

quiz.prompt: Who was Abu ad-Darda joined in brotherhood with, and what is that brotherhood remembered for?

options.text: Bilal ibn Rabah, for teaching him the adhan
Salman al-Farisi, who pulled him back from excess in worship
Zayd ibn Thabit, for helping him copy the Qur'an
Mu'adh ibn Jabal, for sharing the judgeship of Damascus

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra — notice on Abu ad-Darda' among the Companions of Syria
quiz.scholar_reflection: An Ansari trader and a freed Persian, with nothing in common but the reason they were both there. And the useful part of the friendship was the disagreement.

quiz.prompt: What did Abu ad-Darda do in Damascus after Syria was opened?

options.text: He returned to trade on a larger scale
He withdrew to a hermitage outside the city
He served as a judge and taught the Qur'an in its mosque
He commanded the garrison

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra — notice on Abu ad-Darda' among the Companions of Syria; reports differ on which caliph appointed him
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had given up owning property because it distracted him. He then spent years deciding who owned what, in one of the wealthiest cities of the new empire.

quiz.prompt: Which well-known hadith is narrated by Abu ad-Darda?

options.text: 'Actions are only by intentions'
'The scholars are the inheritors of the prophets'
'None of you believes until he loves for his brother'
'Islam began as something strange'

quiz.citation: Sunan Abu Dawud, Book of Knowledge, narrated by Abu ad-Darda'
quiz.scholar_reflection: The same narration says the prophets left no gold or silver, only knowledge. It reaches us through a man who closed his own business.

quiz.prompt: He was among the last of his people to accept Islam, while his own relatives were already at Badr. How do you feel about having come to something late?

options.text: It still embarrasses me more than it should
I have decided the lateness matters less than what happened after
I use it as a reason not to try to catch up
I do not think about it — I only know the pace I am going now

quiz.citation: Reflection on Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, and the reports on his Islam
quiz.scholar_reflection: His first battle was Uhud, not Badr. Nobody who quotes his hadith on knowledge mentions that, and it does not change a word of the narration.

quiz.prompt: He found he could not hold trade and worship together, and chose. Is there something in your life the two hands cannot both carry?

options.text: Yes, and I have known it for a while and done nothing
Yes, and I have already given one of them up
I keep both and do both badly
I think most people can combine them and I am just disorganised

quiz.citation: Reflection on Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra — notice on Abu ad-Darda'
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did not claim it was true for everyone. Other Companions traded until they died and were praised for it. He reported his own limit and acted on it.

quiz.prompt: Salman's usefulness to him was telling him he had gone too far in worship. Who in your life is allowed to say that to you?

options.text: One person, and I sometimes avoid them for it
Nobody, and I have noticed the cost of that
Several people, but I only listen to one of them
I would rather be corrected by a book than by a person

quiz.citation: Reflection on Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, and Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Fasting
quiz.scholar_reflection: Note what the correction was about. Not sin. Excess in something good, which is far harder to hear about, because you can defend it with scripture.

quiz.prompt: He narrated that an angel answers 'and for you the same' when you pray for an absent brother. When did you last pray for someone who has no idea?

options.text: Regularly, by name, and it has changed how I feel about them
Only for people who are ill or in trouble
I say a general du'a and mean nobody in particular
I cannot remember, and that answers the question

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, Book of Remembrance and Supplication, narrated by Abu ad-Darda'
quiz.scholar_reflection: The mechanism in the narration is worth noticing. You are not rewarded for the intention. The angel says it back to you, word for word, while you are still speaking.

quiz.prompt: Little is preserved of his face, his voice or his youth. His legacy is other people: a wife who kept teaching, a city that kept reciting. What would remain of you in that form?

options.text: Something, in one or two people, and I hope it holds
Nothing yet, and I have started thinking about it seriously
I would rather leave something I made than someone I taught
My family, and I am not sure that counts as an achievement

quiz.citation: Reflection on Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, and Sunan Abu Dawud, Book of Knowledge
quiz.scholar_reflection: Umm ad-Darda' went on teaching in Damascus after he died, and the generation after the Companions sat in front of her. Some inheritances only show up one layer down.
